# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML

CORE HYPOTHESIS. Teriflunomide (original indication: relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; the leflunomide parent was approved for rheumatoid/psoriatic arthritis; regulatory facts unverified prior knowledge) reaches clinically achievable free concentrations that inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) in myeloid-primed AML blasts, depleting de novo pyrimidine synthesis (textbook biochemistry, general knowledge) and releasing the differentiation block toward terminal maturation with cell-cycle exit. This is not an LSC-eradication claim and not an established AML regimen.

PRE-REGISTERED EXPOSURE WINDOW (fixes the numeric gap; every number below is unverified prior knowledge requiring label/EPAR and primary-literature verification before any assay). Reported label total Cmax is ~90 µg/mL (~350 µM) with <1% free fraction, giving predicted free trough ~1–2 µM and free Cmax ~2–4 µM. Published DHODH IC50 values for the A77 1726 class (chemically identical to teriflunomide; flagged) span low-nanomolar (cell-free) to ~1–10 µM (whole-cell). Falsifiable go/no-go gate: whole-cell DHODH-engagement EC50 (dihydroorotate:orotate shift plus UTP decline) in primary blasts must be ≤1 µM free-equivalent, ≥2-fold below predicted free trough; if EC50 exceeds 3 µM (above predicted free Cmax), the hypothesis is abandoned before further testing.

SUPPORTED PREMISES. P1 (S4): DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML. P2 (S2): chemotherapy-persistent cells were not LSC-enriched but oxidative-metabolism-dependent. P3 (S1): quiescent ROS-low LSCs carried BCL-2/OXPHOS-linked liabilities; framing only. P4 (S3): venetoclax–azacitidine supplies the established metabolic comparator and biomarker template. No packet source supports teriflunomide efficacy in AML.

NOVELTY POSTURE. The differentiation-via-DHODH concept is imported from S4, and nonclassical DHODH inhibition already received AML clinical testing: brequinar was studied in relapsed/refractory AML in the 1990s with modest single-agent activity and dose-limiting myelosuppression (unverified prior knowledge, to be confirmed). Novelty is therefore confined to drug identity plus an exposure-fitted, biomarker-selected differentiation claim; a literature check for prior teriflunomide/leflunomide AML data gates final promisingness.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES. B1 is the exposure gate above. B2 (now grounded, not asserted): DHODH dependence scales with S-phase pyrimidine demand, so selectivity must be demonstrated against equally cycling normal granulopoietic progenitors; we quantify salvage capacity (SLC29A1/ENT1, UCK1/2) in blasts versus normal CD34+ cells to determine a mechanistic margin. B3: DHODH donates electrons into CoQ, so inhibition may add respiratory stress in the S2 oxidative residual state — secondary endpoint only. B4: differentiation may impair LSC self-renewal without direct killing; otherwise teriflunomide is an add-on.

BOUNDED CONTEXT AND RESPONDER BIOMARKER. Responders are nominated a priori as myeloid-primed states (NPM1-mutant, biallelic CEBPA-mutant); cytostasis-only outcomes are nominated for TP53-mutant and KMT2A-rearranged blasts. Patient selection uses a baseline DHODH-flux signature: pre-treatment dihydroorotate:orotate ratio, [U-13C]-glutamine→UTP de novo flux, and low salvage expression. This genotype-by-flux map is itself a falsifiable prediction, not a universal AML claim.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL STRATEGY. (1) Exposure-matched engagement per the pre-registered gate in a panel spanning NPM1, FLT3-ITD, TP53, and KMT2A-rearranged genotypes. (2) Specificity matrix: uridine rescue must abolish metabolic and differentiative effects; DHODH overexpression or an inhibitor-resistant allele confers resistance; a brequinar-class inhibitor phenocopies; class off-target actions on tyrosine kinases such as JAK3/EGFR at higher concentrations (unverified prior knowledge) are explicitly assayed. (3) Endpoint separation: CD11b/CD14/CD16 induction and NBT reduction versus S-phase exit and apoptosis, benchmarked against a purely cytotoxic control. (4) Selectivity at identical free concentrations: predefined margin of ≤25% normal CD34+ CFU-GM inhibition at concentrations inducing ≥3-fold CD11b/CD14 in ≥70% of blasts, calibrated against brequinar's myelosuppression; exceeding it falsifies the selectivity claim. (5) PDX dosed to human-equivalent free exposure, measuring marrow blast differentiation, DHODH-substrate accumulation, and survival on the S3 analytic template. (6) Combination testing (HMA or venetoclax) in S2-like residual disease only after single-agent validation, with S3 as comparator, never as the proposal.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS. At clinically matched free exposure: (a) EC50 outside the pre-registered window (>3 µM); (b) DHODH engagement without differentiation (only cytostasis/apoptosis); (c) differentiation not rescued by uridine and unmodified by DHODH genetic state; (d) >25% normal CD34+ colony inhibition at differentiating concentrations; (e) no correlation between baseline de novo-flux signature and response across genotypes, disproving the responder-biomarker claim; (f) genotype-outcome behavior opposite to the nomination.

LIMITATIONS. Multi-week half-life implies slow pharmacodynamics (label detail to verify); class risks — immunosuppression, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity — require label confirmation; murine xenografts poorly model human uridine salvage; whether teriflunomide/leflunomide was previously tested in AML cannot be verified from the packet, so novelty must be re-scoped if such data exist; all exposure and IC50 numbers are provisional until verified; investigational DHODH inhibitors are not approved drugs and neither satisfy nor pre-empt this repurposing question.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML
